These recent EC effect findings with (PVDF-TrFE-CFE) encourage further development of these materials for solid-state cooling applications. One disadvantage of current polymeric EC materials is that the bulk materials have a large electrode spacing and require large electric fields, which challenges the safe operation of electrocaloric devices. Another option for the design of EC materials in electrocaloric devices is multilayer chips (MLCs). However, the structure of MLCs are not well-developed for EC devices, and it is not easily amenable to manufacturing.1 Thus, thin films may be a solution to avoid the need to apply large electric fields during the EC cycle, and they may be easier to manufacture at a commercial scale for practical applications. In addition, the thin film possesses a fast heat conduction, and the EC effect can be triggered easily at a lower applied field.1,16,17 Moreover, polymer thin films can withstand extremely high fields and produce higher electrocaloric temperature change,18 enhance film breakdown strength, and reduce film defects.19 This further encourages the thin film fabrication for EC materials. To date, most EC experiments have focused on polymer thin film prepared by solution casting. Traditional solution casting the polymer requires extended periods of time (e.g., hours to days) to evaporate solvent and is therefore not ideal for commercial manufacturing, but this can be adapted to be scalable (e.g., blade casting and bar casting) in industries. Other research has demonstrated that alternative processing methods, including electrospining13 and spin-casting8, can produce PVDF-TrFE-CFE films with a large EC effect. While spin casting does generate thin films, it is not a scalable and continuous manufacturing process.
